Slides (black), the lecture notes (green — study guide written from Dr. Alghamdi's lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). Aldughaither has no mediastinum chapter.

Objectives

  • Anatomy · contents of the compartments · imaging · surgical and endoscopic access · mediastinal conditions: masses, mediastinal infections, pneumomediastinum.

1. Anatomy — the compartments

  • Divided into superior, anterior, middle and posterior compartments.
  • Superior: above the line from the 4th thoracic vertebra to the sternomanubrial junction (angle of Louis).
  • Anterior: between the posterior sternum and the pericardium.
  • Middle: bounded by the pericardium anteriorly and posteriorly.
  • Posterior: from the posterior pericardium to the longitudinal spinal ligament (vertebral column).

Mediastinal compartments — superior, anterior, middle and posterior (diagram and lateral chest X-ray)

  • Mediastinal tumours most commonly occur in the ANTERIOR compartment; the MIDDLE is the least common.
  • Lymph nodes are found in all compartments, most commonly anterior (lymphoma); sarcoidosis → middle compartment.
  • The pericardium is the practical landmark. Frequency: anterior (most) > posterior > middle (least). Lymph nodes are the most common mediastinal mass overall.
SuperiorAnterior — most commonMiddle — least commonPosterior
Retrosternal goitreThymomaBronchogenic cystNeurogenic tumour
ThymomaLymphomaMediastinal lymphadenopathyBony osteophyte
Thymic cystGerm cell tumourPericardial cystOesophageal duplication cyst
ParathyroidThymic cystSaccular aneurysm of the PAOesophageal leiomyoma
  • Notes add — anterior/superior: thyroid/ectopic parathyroid (persistent ↑PTH after parathyroidectomy → suspect an ectopic gland in the thymus), thymic hyperplasia/thymoma/carcinoma/cyst/thymolipoma, germ cell tumours · posterior: large hiatal hernia, oesophageal tumours (leiomyoma, GIST), thoracic-duct cyst, ectopic adrenal/paraganglionic tissue.
  • Asymptomatic young man, rounded left paravertebral (posterior) mass at T12 → neurofibroma (neurogenic tumour). 437 ×9
  • Cough + mild dysphagia, enlarged right thyroid lobe, CXR mass in the superior mediastinum (retrosternal goitre) → CT chest and neck. 438 ×11

Mediastinal lymphadenopathy (notes)

CategoryCauses
Primary — malignantLymphoma
Primary — infectiousTB; viral (EBV, CMV, HIV); fungal (aspergillosis)
Primary — inflammatorySarcoidosis, SLE, RA, vasculitis
SecondaryMetastatic cancer, especially lung
  • Sarcoidosis: more common in people of African descent and women, middle age, middle compartment (hilar/peribronchial nodes). Lymphoma: classically anterior. HIV can itself cause marked lymphadenopathy.
  • 45-year-old Black African, SOB, splenomegaly, multiple peribronchial lymphadenopathy → sarcoidosis. 439

2. Presentation

  • Asymptomatic: incidental finding on imaging.
  • Symptomatic: higher risk of malignancy; symptoms come from compression of structures, invasion, or paraneoplastic syndrome.
  • When you find a mediastinal mass always ask for: ACh-receptor antibodies · serum tumour markers (AFP, β-HCG, LDH) · in males, testicular ultrasound.
  • Adults: usually asymptomatic and benign. Children: more often symptomatic and malignant.
Structure compressed/invadedSymptom
TracheaDyspnoea
Recurrent laryngeal nerveHoarseness
OesophagusDysphagia
PericardiumEffusion ± tamponade
Pleura / chest wallEffusion, pleuritic pain
  • Anterior mediastinal mass work-up (memorize): AChR antibodies (myasthenia/thymoma) · LDH (lymphoma) · AFP and β-hCG (germ cell tumours) · testicular US in males (exclude a testicular primary with mediastinal mets).
  • Young man, incidental anterior mediastinal mass with raised β-hCG and AFP → next step testicular ultrasound. 442

3. Imaging

  • Chest X-ray.
  • CT chest: the most important modality.
  • MRI: superior to CT for vascular or structural invasion · differentiates solid vs cystic · ESSENTIAL for posterior-compartment tumours — neurogenic tumours with intraspinal components.
  • PET/PET-CT: important for lymphoma staging.
  • EUS ± EBUS — done by the endoscopist.
  • Contrast CT = gold standard. PET is not routine for every mass and is not required for germ cell tumours. Oesophageal leiomyoma: avoid biopsy if imaging is typical (it makes later enucleation harder).
  • Headache and arm weakness with a posterior mediastinal mass → spinal MRI (rule out intraspinal "dumbbell" extension). 439

4. Surgical access to the mediastinum

CompartmentAccess
AnteriorVATS · robotic (RATS) · median sternotomy · Chamberlain procedure (anterior mediastinotomy)
MiddleCervical mediastinoscopy · extended cervical mediastinoscopy · Chamberlain · VATS · RATS
PosteriorThoracotomy · VATS · RATS
  • Chamberlain = historical anterior mediastinotomy for station 5 (aortopulmonary window) nodes. Cervical mediastinoscopy = incision in the neck, along the trachea, biopsy of paratracheal nodes.
  • Biopsy of an anterior mediastinal mass → CT-guided biopsy (mediastinoscopy reaches the middle/paratracheal nodes, not the anterior mediastinum). 436 ×2

5. Thymus

  • Thymomas: associated with myasthenia gravis, agammaglobulinaemia, and red-cell aplasia.
  • Other lesions: thymic cancers · thymic hyperplasia · thymic cysts · thymic carcinoid · thymic lipoma.
  • Identify associated haematological disease before thymectomy — risk of significant perioperative bleeding.

Myasthenia gravis

  • An autoimmune disorder of skeletal muscle caused by IgG antibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (AChR) of the motor end-plate.
  • Ranges from intermittent ocular weakness to severe generalized weakness and respiratory depression.
  • Managed primarily by neurologists: anticholinesterases (pyridostigmine, neostigmine) and immunomodulators (corticosteroids, azathioprine).
  • Plasmapheresis removes antibodies → rapid short-term improvement (within days, lasts a few weeks) — for myasthenic crisis or refractory disease. Alternative: IVIG.
  • Most patients with MG who undergo thymectomy improve or reach complete remission over several years.
  • Strong evidence also supports thymectomy in non-thymomatous MG.
  • Fatigable weakness, ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia; respiratory arrest from respiratory or bulbar weakness. MG = postsynaptic (AChR antibodies); Lambert-Eaton = presynaptic (voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel antibodies); Guillain-Barré = ascending peripheral neuropathy (Campylobacter).
  • Crisis: plasmapheresis is faster than IVIG. High-risk MG before surgery: admit → 2 doses IVIG → operate ~7 days later.
  • MG + thymoma → thymectomy. Response in thirds: ⅓ remission, ⅓ improve with less medication, ⅓ little change. Non-thymomatous MG thymectomy selection: age 18 to < 60, symptoms < 5 years, good response to medication — minimally invasive (VATS/robotic).
  • Ptosis, diplopia, positive Tensilon test and a homogeneous anterior mediastinal mass → myasthenia gravis with thymoma. 439 ×4
  • MG with a 6.5 × 7 cm thymoma → surgical approach keyed VATS thymectomy (complete thymectomy; sternotomy for large invasive tumours). 438 ×3

6. Germ cell tumours

  • Most originate in the gonads, but 5–10% arise in the anterior mediastinum — the second most common site.
  • Types: teratoma · seminomatous (PMSGCT) · nonseminomatous (PMNSGCT).

Teratoma

  • Unlike malignant germ cell tumours (almost all male), mature teratomas occur equally in both sexes; most present in infancy or childhood — chest pain, then dyspnoea and cough.
  • A cystic part can become infected; rupture into the pleura or tracheobronchial tree → expectoration of hair or sebum (pathognomonic).
  • CT: a mass; about half show calcification, sometimes recognizable bone or teeth.
  • AFP and β-HCG should be obtained but are usually normal.
  • Benign teratomas don't respond to radiation or chemotherapy → with typical CT and normal markers, complete surgical excision without biopsy.
  • Teratoma pearl: hair/teeth/fat on CT + normal markers → excise without biopsy (biopsy only if NSGCT is also suspected). Ruptured teratoma → antibiotics, chest tube, CT, bronchoscopy; operate early if feasible.
  • Anterior mass with calcification, teeth and bone, normal AFP/β-hCG → teratoma. 442
  • Mediastinal mass containing fat and bone, stable → surgical resection. 442 ×2

Seminoma (PMSGCT)

  • Histology like testicular seminoma; exclusively young adult males, 20–40; chest pain, dyspnoea, cough.
  • CT: bulky, lobulated but HOMOGENEOUS mass; occasional invasion. Metastases to cervical nodes, lung, liver, bone.
  • Pure seminoma usually has normal tumour markers.
  • Cisplatin-based chemotherapy (BEP — bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin).
  • Unlike NSGCT, a residual mass after chemotherapy is usually just necrosis → surgery not indicated.
  • 40-year-old man, anterior mediastinal mass, negative markers, homogeneous on CT → seminoma. 439

Nonseminomatous germ cell tumour (PMNSGCT)

  • Worse prognosis — "poor risk".
  • Types: yolk sac (most common), embryonal carcinoma, choriocarcinoma (least common) — often mixed with teratoma.
  • CT: large HETEROGENEOUS mass with necrosis and haemorrhage; local invasion (lung, great veins, pericardium) is common.
  • Raised serum AFP is diagnostic of PMNSGCT — no histology needed.
  • Metastases in 20–25% before chemo — lung most common, then cervical nodes, liver, bone, CNS.
  • Four cycles of cisplatin-based BEP (risk of O₂ toxicity with bleomycin) → when markers normalize, surgery ~6 weeks after chemo.
  • Growing teratoma: paradoxical growth of a cystic mass compressing adjacent organs while tumour markers normalize during chemo → stop chemotherapy and operate.
  • BEP — bleomycin → pulmonary fibrosis; high-concentration oxygen precipitates bleomycin lung injury. NSGCT is usually not operated first — chemo first to improve resectability.
  • NSGCT on chemo: mass enlarging while markers normalize → growing teratoma syndrome. 442
  • 18-year-old on chemo for an anterior mediastinal mass, worse SOB after the 2nd cycle with normalizing markers → nonseminoma (growing teratoma component). 439

Lymphoma (from past exams)

  • Young man, fever, night sweats, weight loss, heterogeneous anterior mass, Reed-Sternberg cells (Hodgkin lymphoma) → chemotherapy (not surgery). 437 ×6

7. Middle compartment

  • Bronchogenic and oesophageal cysts: bronchogenic cysts are commonly symptomatic; oesophageal cysts are asymptomatic. Complete excision is the treatment of choice (increasing size, symptoms or complications).
  • Pericardial cysts: congenital; surgical resection is preferred over aspiration, especially when enlarging or symptomatic.
  • Both foregut cysts come from abnormal separation of trachea and oesophagus: bronchogenic → middle, oesophageal duplication → posterior. Pericardial cyst: ~70% right-sided; excise — aspiration alone tends to recur.
  • CT: a thin, fluid-filled structure next to the heart → pericardial cyst. 442
  • Homogeneous cystic superior mediastinal mass adjacent to the trachea → bronchogenic cyst. 437 ×3

8. Neurogenic tumours

  • Adults: commonly nerve-sheath origin, the majority benign — one fifth of all mediastinal tumours: schwannomas, neurofibromas, malignant schwannomas (neurogenic sarcomas).
  • Children and young adults: tumours of the autonomic ganglia, frequently malignant — ganglioneuroma, ganglioneuroblastoma, neuroblastoma.
  • Mediastinal phaeochromocytoma (< 2% of all): paroxysmal or sustained hypertension; diagnosis by urinary catecholamines and metabolites.
  • Von Recklinghausen's neurofibromatosis is the only known predisposing factor.
  • Surgery dominates treatment.
  • Intraspinal extension must be recognized pre-operatively → combined posterior spinal + thoracic approach (dumbbell tumours).
  • Dumbbell tumour: extends through an intervertebral foramen into the spinal canal — MRI is essential before surgery; operate with the spine/neurosurgery team.

9. Mediastinitis

  • Deep cervical fascial layers divide the neck into retrovisceral, pretracheal and perivascular spaces — each communicates with the mediastinum.
  • Most common pathway: retrovisceral space → posterior mediastinum.
  • Pretracheal route → anterior, retrosternal → pleural/pericardial involvement (purulent pericarditis, tamponade).
  • Perivascular (carotid sheath) → cranial-nerve palsies and massive haemorrhage from vessel erosion.

Acute necrotizing mediastinitis (ANM)

  • Life-threatening. Sources: odontogenic, peritonsillar or other pharyngeal infections; post-sternotomy; oropharyngeal/oesophageal perforation, paraoesophageal hernia with gastric perforation, cervical trauma, sternoclavicular joint infection, pancreatic infection tracking up, misplaced central line, IV drug use.
  • Diagnosis: CT neck and chest — fluid collections, air bubbles, tissue thickening.
  • Treatment: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin–tazobactam, covering oropharyngeal aerobes and anaerobes) + urgent debridement and drainage.
  • Like necrotizing fasciitis of the mediastinum; ~50% mortality. Clue: fever, hypotension, tachycardia, bilateral effusions + poor dentition/neck infection → urgent CT. Antibiotics alone are not enough — repeated debridement (e.g. every 48 h).
  • Fever, chest pain, neck swelling after a dental infection, air in the mediastinum → descending necrotizing mediastinitis. 442

10. Pneumomediastinum

  • Air in the mediastinal space. The most common source is extension of air from the lung — alveolar rupture from deep respiratory manoeuvres, asthma, vomiting (especially in pregnancy), mechanical ventilation (barotrauma) or trauma → air tracks to the hilum and mediastinum.
  • Traumatic rupture of the trachea/main bronchi and oesophageal perforation are less common but more serious causes.

Treatment

  • Asymptomatic, no concern for airway or oesophageal injury → no treatment necessary.
  • Oesophageal perforation (life-threatening): contained → conservative (NPO + IV antibiotics); not contained → NPO, IV antibiotics, chest tube, OR for repair and drainage.
  • Airway injury (traumatic or iatrogenic): suspected with a constant air leak from the chest tube and a non-expanding lung → intubate over a bronchoscope (assess the airway and intubate beyond the injury) → surgical repair.
  • Also with DKA + vomiting, hyperemesis gravidarum. Uncomplicated → oxygen, analgesia, observation. Boerhaave = spontaneous rupture after forceful vomiting: contained → conservative with reassessment (~72 h); free leak → urgent surgery.
  • Coughing then neck pain, pneumomediastinum → extension of air from the lung. 441
  • Stable, pneumomediastinum, endoscopy shows a contained oesophageal leak → NPO + IV antibiotics (conservative). 441

Mastery checklist (notes)

  • Compartments are defined by the pericardium; anterior masses are most common.
  • Sarcoidosis → middle (African descent, women, 50s); lymphoma → anterior.
  • Anterior mass in a male: AChR antibodies, LDH, AFP, β-hCG, testicular US.
  • Contrast CT is the gold standard; MRI for dumbbell tumours; PET not routine for germ cell tumours.
  • Teratoma: hair/teeth/fat + normal markers → excise without biopsy.
  • Seminoma: homogeneous, normal markers, BEP (no surgery). NSGCT: heterogeneous, ↑AFP/β-hCG, chemo then resection.
  • Growing teratoma syndrome: markers improve, mass grows → stop chemo, resect.
  • Check for haematological paraneoplastic disease before thymectomy.
  • Myasthenic crisis: plasmapheresis is faster than IVIG; LEMS is presynaptic, MG postsynaptic.
  • Retrovisceral space = commonest route of descending infection.
  • ANM: antibiotics + drainage + urgent debridement (~50% mortality).
  • Most pneumomediastinum = alveolar air leak; rule out oesophageal/airway injury.
  • Persistent major air leak despite a chest tube → tracheobronchial injury → bronchoscopy.
  • Pericardial cysts are excised, not aspirated.
